```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
library(lazer)
```

lazer gathers the readers and writers of day-to-day work, so a team has
one place for them and new readers can be added there. They share three
habits: they are quiet when all is well, they report every problem in one
message, and they never drop or reinterpret data without saying so.

## Many files at once: `read_files()`

Reading a set of files normally takes a small pipeline: `list.files()`, a
loop or `purrr::map()`, and manual naming. `read_files()` does it in one
call: it expands paths with glue syntax, checks that *every* file exists
before reading anything, picks the reader from the extension, and names
the results. A single path returns the object directly; several return a
named list.

```{r}
df  <- read_files("data/results.parquet")
lst <- read_files("data/dat{0:9}.parquet", names = 0:9)
```

Supported formats: `csv`, `tsv`, `parquet`, `feather`, `xlsx`, `xls`,
`rds`, `sas7bdat`, `sav`, `por`, `xpt`, `dta`, `json`, `ndjson`, `jsonl`,
`yaml`, `yml`, `txt`. CSV files are read as semicolon-separated with a
decimal comma, the Danish convention; pass `reader = readr::read_csv` for
comma-separated files. Any reader works:

```{r}
read_files("data/dat{0:9}.parquet",
           reader = \(x) arrow::read_parquet(x, col_select = 1:5))
```

A file that fails to read does not stop the others; all failures are
reported together at the end, each with its file. Column names are
lowercased by default (`.lowercase = FALSE` to keep them).

**Binding.** `out = "bind"` stacks the files, and `.id` records where each
row came from (numeric when `names` is). When a column's types cannot be
combined across files, a warning names it, and only that column is
re-typed with `readr::parse_guess()`; every other column keeps its type.
`daos::view_types()` shows which file differs.

```{r}
read_files("data/dat{2020:2024}.parquet", names = 2020:2024,
           out = "bind", .id = "year")
```

**Unpacking.** `out = "unpack"` assigns each file as its own variable in
the calling environment, and refuses to overwrite existing ones unless
`.overwrite = TRUE`.

```{r}
read_files("data/dat{0:9}.parquet", names = paste0("dat", 0:9), out = "unpack")
```

## Excel: `read_workbook()` and `inspect_excel()`

`readxl::read_excel()` reads one sheet, and on that sheet the smallest
rectangle around *every* non-empty cell. In a published workbook that
means the title becomes the header, the source note becomes a row, and a
comment to the right becomes a column named `...7`. `read_workbook()`
reads every sheet into a named list and finds the table on each: the
largest block of cells not split by an empty row or column, with title
rows on top left out. Whatever lies outside is not read, and one warning
says what and where:

```{r}
sheets <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx")
#> Warning: 'report.xlsx': cells outside the area read on 1 sheet were not read:
#> * Report: F4 right of B3:C6 ("note")
#> * Report: B9 below B3:C6 ("Source: DST")
```

Choose the area yourself when needed: a range, one per sheet (`NA` keeps
the automatic one), a named range from the workbook, or a defined Excel
table, which keeps its range when rows are added.

```{r}
df     <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = "Report!B3:F40")
sheets <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = c(Report = "B3:F40", Notes = NA))
sales  <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = "Salesdata")   # Name Manager
tables <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", table = TRUE)
```

`inspect_excel()` runs the same check without reading and returns the
blocks as a tibble, empty when the layout is clean, so it can serve as a
checkpoint before a scheduled read.

Everything is read with readxl's fast reader, twice: once as text to find
the table, once for the table itself. Password-protected workbooks cannot
be read by readxl; `read_workbook()` says so instead of failing with a zip
error.

## Presentable Excel output: `write_excel()`

This function exists because a plain data export is hard to read for the
people the file is meant for. The complaint from a colleague who works
with macroeconomic statistics was concrete: no frozen header, no thousand
separators, no rounding. `writexl::write_xlsx()` is fast but writes exactly
such unformatted files, and `openxlsx2` can do all the styling but wants a
workbook object, worksheets, styles and a save call. `write_excel()` sits
in between: one call, with defaults that make the file presentable.

- Numeric columns with at least one absolute value of 1,000 or more get a
  thousand separator and no displayed decimals (`#,##0`); the stored values
  are not rounded. `digits = 2` shows two decimals, `digits = NULL` turns
  the formatting off.
- Year-like columns are left alone: a numeric column where every value is
  a whole number between 1800 and 2200 is taken for years, so `2020` is not
  shown as `2.020`. Turn it off with `detect_years = FALSE`, and use
  `skip_fmt` for columns the rule cannot guess (e.g. period codes like
  `202001`).
- `NA` is a blank cell, the header row is bold, and the first row is frozen
  (`freeze_header = FALSE` to turn it off).

Only `.xlsx` can be written; another extension fails early.

```{r}
write_excel(mtcars, "output.xlsx")                              # sheet "Sheet1"
write_excel(list(Cars = mtcars, Iris = iris), "output.xlsx")    # one sheet each
```

`mode = "append"` adds sheets to an existing file and fails on a name that
is taken; `mode = "replace"` replaces matching sheets and adds new ones,
keeping their positions; `mode = "overwrite"` replaces the whole file.
Sheet names are matched ignoring case.

```{r}
write_excel(list(Bilag = iris), "output.xlsx", mode = "append")
write_excel(list(Cars = mtcars), "output.xlsx", mode = "replace")
write_excel(mtcars, "output.xlsx", as_table = TRUE)    # filter arrows, banded rows
```

## Microsoft Access: `read_access()`

Connects to an `.mdb` or `.accdb` file via ODBC, runs a SQL query and
returns a tibble. Needs the `DBI` and `odbc` packages and an Access ODBC
driver. `verbosity` is `"compact"` (one line per file, the default),
`"full"` or `"quiet"`.

```{r}
df <- read_access("data/sales.mdb", "SELECT * FROM Customers")
```

## Greenlandic TA files

There are two layouts: version 1, the old one, and version 2, the new
140-character one. `read_ta()` reads both and recognises which by itself.
`write_ta()` writes the one you name, since it has to match the receiver,
and only writes what `read_ta()` reads back unchanged: a value that would
not fit its field, or would lose decimals, is an error listing every such
value, so no file with shifted fields is written. `convert_ta()` converts a
file between the layouts, with the same checks.

```{r}
ta <- read_ta("ta.file")
write_ta(ta, "out.ta", version = 2)
convert_ta("old.ta", "new.ta", to = 2)
```

Both layouts are written as one small table each at the top of `R/ta.R`:
field, start, end, type. The reader and the writer only follow those
tables, so a change in a layout is a change there.
